```{r setup, include=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
```

```{r data}
library(MASS)
data(mcycle)
x <- mcycle$times
y <- mcycle$accel
n <- length(y)
nw_S <- function(x0, x, h) {
  K <- dnorm(outer(x0, x, "-") / h)
  K / rowSums(K)
}
ll_S <- function(x0, x, h) {
  t(sapply(x0, function(u) {
    w <- dnorm((x - u) / h)
    X <- cbind(1, x - u)
    solve(crossprod(X, w * X), t(X * w))[1, ]
  }))
}
```

## 1. A hand-sized example

Five points, triangular kernel $K(u) = (1 - |u|)_+$, bandwidth $h = 2$.
Neighbours at distance 0, 1, 2 get weights 1, 1/2, 0.

```{r toy}
xt <- 1:5
yt <- c(2, 4, 3, 7, 9)
Kt <- pmax(1 - abs(outer(xt, xt, "-")) / 2, 0)
St <- Kt / rowSums(Kt)
St
ft <- drop(St %*% yt)
rt <- yt - ft
c(edf = sum(diag(St)), RSS = sum(rt^2))
cbind(fitted = ft, resid = rt, loo_resid = rt / (1 - diag(St)))
c(LOOCV = mean((rt / (1 - diag(St)))^2),
  GCV = 5 * sum(rt^2) / (5 - sum(diag(St)))^2)
```

## 2. Leave-one-out CV without refitting

For Nadaraya–Watson, local polynomials with a fixed bandwidth and penalized
least squares, the leave-one-out residual is exactly
$(y_i - \hat f_i)/(1 - S_{ii})$. Check it by brute force for $h = 2$.

```{r loo-check}
h <- 2
S <- nw_S(x, x, h)
r <- y - drop(S %*% y)
shortcut <- mean((r / (1 - diag(S)))^2)
brute <- mean(sapply(1:n, function(i) {
  w <- dnorm((x[-i] - x[i]) / h)
  (y[i] - sum(w * y[-i]) / sum(w))^2
}))
c(shortcut = shortcut, brute_force = brute)
```

## 3. Choosing h by LOOCV and GCV

$\mathrm{GCV}(h) = n\,\mathrm{RSS}(h) / (n - \mathrm{tr}\,S_h)^2$ replaces each
$S_{ii}$ by the average $\mathrm{tr}(S_h)/n$.

```{r choose-h}
crit <- function(S) {
  f <- drop(S %*% y); r <- y - f; edf <- sum(diag(S))
  c(edf = edf, LOOCV = mean((r / (1 - diag(S)))^2),
    GCV = n * sum(r^2) / (n - edf)^2)
}
hs <- seq(0.5, 5, by = 0.01)
tab_nw <- t(sapply(hs, function(h) crit(nw_S(x, x, h))))
tab_ll <- t(sapply(hs, function(h) crit(ll_S(x, x, h))))
best <- function(tab, col) c(h = hs[which.min(tab[, col])], tab[which.min(tab[, col]), ])
rbind(NW_LOOCV = best(tab_nw, "LOOCV"), NW_GCV = best(tab_nw, "GCV"),
      LL_LOOCV = best(tab_ll, "LOOCV"), LL_GCV = best(tab_ll, "GCV"))
plot(hs, tab_ll[, "LOOCV"], type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "navy",
     xlab = "bandwidth h", ylab = "criterion", ylim = c(550, 1000))
lines(hs, tab_ll[, "GCV"], lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "navy")
lines(hs, tab_nw[, "LOOCV"], lwd = 2, col = "red")
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c("navy", "navy", "red"), lty = c(1, 2, 1),
       legend = c("local linear LOOCV", "local linear GCV", "NW LOOCV"))
```

## 4. Bias and variance as functions of h

Take a smooth "truth" $f$ (here a heavily smoothed fit to the data, used only
as a test function) and constant $\sigma = 23$. For a linear smoother,
$\mathbb E(\hat f) = S f$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat f) = \sigma^2 S S^\top$, so the
average squared bias and variance can be computed exactly, without simulation.

```{r bias-variance}
f_true <- drop(ll_S(x, x, 2.5) %*% y)   # test function, not an estimate of anything
sigma <- 23
bv <- t(sapply(hs, function(h) {
  S <- nw_S(x, x, h)
  c(bias2 = mean((S %*% f_true - f_true)^2),
    var = sigma^2 * mean(rowSums(S^2)))      # diag(S S') = row sums of squares
}))
mse <- rowSums(bv)
c(h_opt = hs[which.min(mse)], min_MSE = min(mse))
matplot(hs, cbind(bv, mse), type = "l", lty = c(2, 3, 1), lwd = 2,
        col = c("red", "navy", "black"), xlab = "bandwidth h", ylab = "average")
legend("top", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(2, 3, 1), col = c("red", "navy", "black"),
       legend = c("squared bias", "variance", "MSE"))
```

## 5. Comparing smoothers fairly: equal effective df

A bandwidth of 2 means different things for different smoothers. Match them on
$\mathrm{edf} = \mathrm{tr}(S)$ instead. Here every fit uses 12 effective df.

```{r equal-edf}
target <- 12
h_nw <- uniroot(function(h) sum(diag(nw_S(x, x, h))) - target, c(0.5, 5))$root
h_ll <- uniroot(function(h) sum(diag(ll_S(x, x, h))) - target, c(0.5, 5))$root
span <- uniroot(function(s) loess(accel ~ times, mcycle, span = s)$trace.hat - target,
                c(0.2, 0.5))$root
f_nw <- drop(nw_S(x, x, h_nw) %*% y)
f_ll <- drop(ll_S(x, x, h_ll) %*% y)
lo <- loess(accel ~ times, mcycle, span = span)
ss <- smooth.spline(x, y, df = target)
rss <- c(NW = sum((y - f_nw)^2), local_linear = sum((y - f_ll)^2),
         LOESS_quadratic = sum(resid(lo)^2),
         smoothing_spline = sum((y - predict(ss, x)$y)^2))
round(cbind(RSS = rss, GCV = n * rss / (n - target)^2), 1)
round(c(h_nw = h_nw, h_ll = h_ll, span = span), 3)
```

At the same complexity Nadaraya–Watson has the largest residual sum of squares.
Both kernel fits are shallower at the minimum near 20 ms (about −104 g and
−100 g) than LOESS and the smoothing spline (about −115 g): a local constant or
local line has bias proportional to $h^2 f''(x)$ where the curve bends sharply.
Local quadratic fits and splines are close to each other.

## 6. A band of ±2 sd(residuals) is not a confidence band

`sd(resid)` estimates the spread of a **new observation** around $f$; it is
nearly constant in $x$ and ignores the uncertainty of $\hat f$. A pointwise
standard error for $\hat f(x_i)$ under constant variance is
$\hat\sigma\sqrt{(SS^\top)_{ii}}$, which is much narrower and varies with $x$.

```{r bands}
S <- ll_S(x, x, h_ll)
f <- drop(S %*% y)
sigma_hat <- sqrt(sum((y - f)^2) / (n - sum(diag(S))))
se_f <- sigma_hat * sqrt(rowSums(S^2))
c(sigma_hat = sigma_hat, se_f_min = min(se_f), se_f_max = max(se_f))
```

These standard errors still assume constant variance, which the motorcycle
data clearly violate (look at the residuals before 14 ms and between 15 and
40 ms). We return to that in the lab.
